task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent second-half change
H2-H1 change (opponent halftime adjustment) as a team-level trait
split-half and year-to-year reliability of a team effect
regression to the mean and opponent-quality confounding
methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across seasons or across random game splits?
Can a defense trait be separated from opponent quality, game script, regression to the mean and mechanical floor effects?
Is 120 team-seasons enough to detect a reliability of useful size?

historical_evidence.finding: Split-half reliability of connector quality Q_p (n=102 connectors): Pearson r=+0.215, Spearman-Brown about 0.355, ICC 0.216 with 78.4% of variance within-player. Recorded conclusion: too low to treat as a stable scoutable trait. Failure mechanism recorded as A_unanswerable. Risk: MEASURE_RELIABILITY.

Split-half stability of a usage-residual influence measure was high (pooled rho about +0.67 to +0.69). This is a player-property measure, not a defensive H2-H1 effect, and [prior work] is flagged with MEASURE_RELIABILITY.

An adaptation lift (adapter PPP change) was not behaviourally specific: wrong-way and no-signal teams showed similar or larger changes, and there was no carryover to the next game. Recorded failure mechanism is C_artifact, with limits from label error and selection/regression to the mean; risks LABEL_ERROR and MECHANICAL_FLOOR.

H1 usage did not predict H2 suppression beyond mean reversion. Matched effects did not survive BH correction, and top-1 accuracy was 0.550 against a mean-reversion baseline of 0.511. Recorded evidence: the bulk of H2 suppression is regression to the mean (n=8873 team-games). Failure mechanism: B_powered_null.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating a half-split difference-type measure (on-off PPP gap) as a stable attribute
failed_approaches.why: Low split-half reliability (r=0.215, SB about 0.355); most variance is within-unit. Recorded as A_unanswerable / MEASURE_RELIABILITY.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Interpreting an H1-to-H2 PPP change as an adaptation or response effect
failed_approaches.why: Apparent lift was produced by construction, selection and regression to the mean, with label error and mechanical floor effects (C_artifact).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Predicting H2 suppression from H1 features
failed_approaches.why: Most H2 suppression is regression to the mean; lift over the mean-reversion baseline was only +0.039 (B_powered_null).

evidence_establishes: Related H1-to-H2 change measures in this project were dominated by regression to the mean and construction artifacts ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
A difference-type, within-unit contrast measured with split-half methods had low reliability in one earlier family ([prior work][prior work]).
Split-half reliability can be high for some measures (FAM:[prior work]), so low reliability is not guaranteed in general.
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record directly measures the reliability of a team defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change.
[prior work] do not give the between-team variance of that effect or the number of games per team-season needed to detect it.
[prior work] do not show that the effect is zero; they show that naive H2-H1 change is heavily contaminated by regression to the mean and artifacts.
own_inferences: The H2-H1 change is a difference of two noisy halves, so its reliability is likely lower than that of either half. Opponent H1 level mechanically drives H2-H1 through regression to the mean, so the contrast must be residualised before it can be called a defensive effect.
Defense effects on H2-H1 are probably small relative to game-level noise. A true team trait may exist (for example through rotation or fatigue patterns) but be hard to detect.

A team-season has about 82 to 100 games, which is likely enough to estimate a team mean but not a small effect; the number of team-seasons (120) limits the year-to-year reliability test, giving roughly 90 pairs of consecutive seasons.
Any correlation across seasons may be driven by stable team features such as pace, style or roster depth, not a defense-specific suppression effect.
uncertainties: Exact definition of the H2-H1 change (points per possession, points, or efficiency) and whether the effect is on the opponent's offence or the game as a whole.
Whether opponent quality adjustment can be done well with the available data, given that schedules differ by team.
Between-team true variance is unknown; if close to zero, reliability will be low regardless of sample.
Roster turnover across seasons will reduce year-to-year stability even if within-season stability is real.
Garbage time and blowouts can create mechanical H2 effects.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records moved the decision from a plain reliability test to proceeding only with changes: the H2-H1 change must be regression-adjusted and tested against a placebo or permutation baseline, and low reliability is the likely outcome. Records on regression to the mean, artifacts and low split-half reliability made the naive version unattractive, though none tested this exact question.

blocking_constraints.text: A difference-of-halves outcome may have reliability near zero, so the question may reduce to a noise-ceiling result.
Opponent H1 level mechanically predicts H2-H1 change, and a defense's effect must be separated from this.
120 team-seasons gives only about 30 teams over four seasons with year-to-year pairs, limiting precision of reliability estimates.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved family tested whether a defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait. Related families show regression to the mean dominating H1-to-H2 change ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]) and low reliability for a difference-type measure ([prior work][prior work]). They inform the design but do not answer the question.

risks.text: H2-H1 is a difference score. Reliability should be estimated with game-level random splits and with cross-season correlation, and compared to a noise ceiling.
Opponent H1 performance determines H2-H1 through regression to the mean. Model H2 on H1 and expected level instead of using raw differences.
Opponent quality, home/away, rest, pace, game score, and the defense's own H1 performance can all drive H2-H1 change. Include them as covariates or fixed effects.
Garbage time, blowouts and score-dependent substitutions and fouling produce mechanical H2 changes unrelated to defense. Restrict to close games or condition on margin at half.
Rule changes, league scoring trends and roster turnover across 2022-26 can change both the baseline and team identity.
Few team-seasons limit between-team reliability precision; a CI on reliability will probably be wide.
Reliability should be compared against a shuffled-team placebo, or a trait claim may only reflect general features such as pace.

design.estimand: Between-team variance share (ICC) and split-half / cross-season correlation of a defense's residualised effect on opponent H2-H1 change, defined as opponent H2 points per 100 possessions minus the value predicted from opponent H1 efficiency, season-level opponent strength, home/away and rest. The estimand is the correlation of team defense effects between independent halves of the games or between seasons.
design.unit: Team-season (defense), with games as repeated observations within it.
design.sample: All 120 team-seasons from the 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons, with playoffs analysed separately and not pooled. Exclude games where the margin at half exceeds a pre-set threshold (for example 20) and treat overtime separately.
design.power: With about 82 games per team-season, a mixed-effects model estimates between-team variance. Pre-specify the minimum reliability of interest at a Spearman-Brown value of at least 0.4 for a 'reliable' trait. The cross-season correlation with about 90 consecutive pairs has a 95% CI of roughly +/-0.2, so only r above about 0.3 is detectable. Run a simulation using observed game-level SD to confirm the expected noise ceiling before analysis.
design.controls: Opponent H1 efficiency (to model regression to the mean), opponent season offensive rating, home/away, rest days, pace, margin at half, and the defense's season-level defensive rating. Also report results with and without the controls.
design.falsification: (1) Permutation test: shuffle defensive team labels across games within season and compare the observed ICC and split-half r to the null. (2) Placebo outcome: apply the same pipeline to H1 versus H2 of a random pair of quarters. (3) Check whether the estimate collapses to defensive rating or pace alone.
design.multiplicity: One primary test (odd/even game split-half reliability of the residualised effect, Spearman-Brown corrected). Secondary tests: cross-season correlation, playoffs separately. Apply Holm correction across the secondary tests.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the primary SB reliability is at least 0.4 with a lower 95% CI bound above 0.2, permutation p<0.05, and the cross-season correlation is positive with CI excluding 0. Rejected if the upper CI bound of SB reliability is below 0.25 (powered null). Otherwise report inconclusive. If the effect vanishes after residualising for regression to the mean, label it an artifact.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and box-score files for 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons, as available on 2026-10-06 (2025-26 regular season and playoffs complete). Freeze the data snapshot and pre-register the code before analysis.
